title: Accretive Health / A.H. Belo / Apollo Healthcare / Allied Healthcare / AdaptHealth — Time Decay, Strategic Value and Per-Share Compounding V9

notes: Raw Short -> actual Long corrections: A.H. Belo 2010, 2012, 2013, 2016, 2017 and Apollo Healthcare 2020.
AHC and AHC. are different companies: AHC is A.H. Belo while AHC. in 2020 is Apollo Healthcare.
No usable source-DB performance rows were found for any of the ten Batch 76 ideas.
A.H. Belo became DallasNews and completed a 1-for-4 reverse split in 2021, so the 2025 Hearst $16.50 cash takeout equals $4.125 on the pre-split share basis.
A.H. Belo 2012 and 2013 are the strongest vintages because non-core assets were monetized quickly and $3.75/share of special dividends was returned.
A.H. Belo 2016 and 2017 correctly identified hard real-estate value but underestimated print-franchise erosion and time decay.
Apollo Healthcare was acquired for C$4.50 cash/share, only modestly above the roughly C$3.9-C$4.0 implied VIC entry and far below the C$14.20 base target.
Allied Healthcare was acquired by Saga for $3.90 cash/share; the 2009 $1.20 entry generated about +225%, while the 2010 implied ~$2.49 entry generated about +57%.
AdaptHealth expanded revenue and adjusted EBITDA materially but suffered large goodwill impairments and severe per-share value destruction.
Accretive Health 2013 demonstrates that executive recruitment is weaker evidence than audited reporting, auditor sign-off and filing compliance.

batch_lessons: Executive recruitment is weaker evidence than audited financial statements, auditor sign-off and timely filings.
Melting-ice-cube SOTP requires explicit time decay: hard assets can be real while the operating franchise erodes faster.
A.H. Belo's best vintages were those in which asset sales and special dividends arrived quickly, not those with the largest static SOTP.
Reverse splits must be adjusted before comparing historical entry prices with terminal takeout prices.
Ticker punctuation can distinguish completely different issuers; AHC and AHC. must not be merged.
A successful operating turnaround does not validate an aggressive normalized-earnings multiple; Apollo's C$4.50 takeout is the strongest private-market falsifier.
The same strategic exit produces radically different returns at different entry prices, as Allied Healthcare's 2009 and 2010 vintages show.
M&A compounders should be evaluated on per-share free cash flow and acquisition ROIC, not consolidated revenue or adjusted EBITDA growth.
Large goodwill impairments are useful ex-post evidence that acquisition prices or expected synergies were too aggressive.
A structural industry tailwind cannot rescue bad capital allocation or an overvalued entry.
